opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this question a lot, especially since moving from research into building a company.

To me, a good business starts with solving a real problem for real people, something they genuinely care about, not something that only looks interesting on paper. As engineers and researchers, it's easy to fall in love with the technology itself. I've been guilty of that. You build something elegant and powerful, and you assume people will come. But a good business is not about how clever the technology is. It's about whether it creates value that someone is willing to pay for, repeatedly.

The second thing is that the value should be sustainable. Can you deliver it in a way that scales? Do your costs go down as you grow, or do they grow with every customer? Software and AI are interesting because, done right, the marginal cost can be very low, so you can serve a huge number of users with a small team. That leverage is very powerful.

Third, I think a good business needs some kind of compounding advantage. That could be technology, data, brand, community, or just the speed at which your team learns and iterates. In a fast-moving field like AI, I actually think iteration speed is one of the most underrated moats. The landscape changes every few months, so the ability to listen to users, ship quickly, and correct mistakes matters more than any single feature.

And finally, honestly, a good business is one where the people building it believe in what they're doing. Startups are hard. There will be many moments when things don't work. If the team is aligned around a mission they care about, like, for us, making 3D content creation accessible to everyone, that gives you the resilience to keep going.

So, simply put: real user value, a scalable way to deliver it, something that compounds over time, and a team that truly cares. If you have those, you have a good chance of building something meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses solving real user problems and creating value, but does not identify recognizing a market others doubt exists.

r002.rationale: It mentions a compounding advantage and iteration speed as a moat, but does not say that lacking an advantage makes a business vulnerable to better-resourced competitors taking its market.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I've thought about a lot since moving from academia into building a company, and I think my answer has changed over time.

When I was doing research, I used to think a good business was basically a good technology with a price tag on it. You build something impressive, people see how impressive it is, and they pay you. That turned out to be mostly wrong. Taichi was a very capable system, and I'm proud of the engineering, but capability alone doesn't make a business. The question that actually matters is whether you're solving a problem that someone feels acutely, and whether they feel it badly enough to change how they work and pay you to fix it.

So the first thing I'd say is: a good business is anchored to a real, painful problem, not to a clever solution looking for one. Engineers, myself included, tend to get this backwards. We fall in love with the solution.

The second thing is that the value you create has to be captured, not just created. There are lots of things that create enormous value in the world and capture almost none of it. Open source is a beautiful example. We created a lot of value with Taichi, and most of it rightly went to users, which was fine for the mission, but a business needs a mechanism to keep some of that value so it can keep investing. If you don't have that loop, you have a project, not a business. It can be a great project. But it will eventually run out of oxygen.

Third, and this is the one I underestimated the most, is distribution. A good business has a repeatable way to reach the people who need it. If every customer requires a heroic effort to find and convince, you don't really have a business yet, you have a series of lucky events. Repeatability is what separates the two.

And then there's the human side. A good business is one where the people inside it would choose to be there even if they had other options, and where the customers would be genuinely sad if you disappeared. That second test is one I keep coming back to. If you shut down tomorrow and nobody really missed you, that tells you something important.

Finally, I'd say a good business is honest about its unit economics early. It's easy to hide behind growth or behind a big vision, and I've seen that in myself. But at some point the math has to work: what it costs you to serve a customer versus what they pay you over time. If that math works, almost everything else is fixable. If it doesn't, no amount of good technology will save you.

So, in short: a real painful problem, a way to capture some of the value you create, a repeatable path to customers, people who would miss you, and honest economics. The technology is necessary, but it's usually the least differentiating part, which is a humbling thing for someone like me to admit.

r001.rationale: The response says a good business solves an acute, painful problem, but does not identify recognizing a market others do not believe exists.

r002.rationale: The response discusses value capture, distribution, and unit economics, but does not say that lacking a competitive advantage exposes a business to better-resourced competitors.

astra-6.text:
I think a good business creates something people really need and finds a sustainable way to deliver it. Those are two separate challenges. You can build something technically impressive, but if it doesn’t solve a meaningful problem for a customer, it’s hard to make a business out of it. And you can solve a real problem but spend more delivering the solution than customers are willing to pay.

So I would ask: How much value are we creating? Can we capture enough of that value to keep improving the product? And is there a reason customers will continue choosing us? If those things reinforce each other, I think you have the foundation of a good business.

r002.rationale: It asks whether customers have a reason to keep choosing the business, but does not state that lacking a competitive advantage exposes it to better-resourced competitors taking its market.

sol-6.1.text: I think a good business creates real value for its customers and captures enough of that value to keep improving. People choose your product because it solves a problem for them, and they keep coming back. And ideally, as the business grows, you can serve more people without the cost and complexity growing just as fast. So I would look at customer value, sustainable economics, and the ability to scale.
